about: mDNS, RFC 6762 — DNS message format (RFC 1035 §4.1) carried on UDP 5353 to 224.0.0.251.
This describes the QUERY, which is one of the two formats RFC 6762 uses and the one whose
structure is settled by the description rather than by a count on the wire. What is here is the
DNS header, one question, and the thing every DNS message is made of: a NAME, which is a run of
length-prefixed labels ending at a label of length zero.
As many questions as QDCOUNT says, each with a name of its own — which is a run inside a run, and
the reason this is worth having as a worked example: nothing else here needs one.
What is deliberately NOT here is the response, and the reason is worth stating rather than leaving
as an absence. A response's names may be COMPRESSED (§18.14, RFC 1035 §4.1.4): a name may end in a
two-octet pointer holding an absolute offset into the message, and going out a position is only
settled after every value is — so nothing can be derived from one. That is an ordering the engine
could have and does not, rather than anything mDNS asks for that a description could not say.
So the scope is stated in the octets rather than in this paragraph: QR and the three record counts
are checked, and a response, or a query carrying answers (§7.1 known-answer suppression), is
refused where it is written rather than read as though the extra parts were not sent.

nodes.about: RFC 6762 §5.1. QR=0. One question, asked of everyone on the link.
RFC 1035 §4.1.1, unchanged by mDNS — twelve octets, six sixteen-bit words.

about: RFC 6762 §18.1: in multicast queries the Query Identifier SHOULD be zero. SHOULD, not MUST — a
legacy unicast query carries a real one and is answered with it echoed back — so this is an
input rather than a constant, and the capture's zero is a value it was given.

nodes.about: RFC 1035 §4.1.1's second word. Ten fields, sixteen bits, and each one is its own node.
Query or response. Zero here, and that is what makes this message a query rather than something a flag decides partway through reading it.

nodes.label: QR is zero in a query

nodes.about: Nought, and nothing else.
RFC 6762 §18.3: MUST be zero on transmission in a query, and a query with any other opcode MUST be silently ignored.
RFC 6762 §18.4: zero on transmission in a query, ignored on reception.

about: RFC 6762 §18.5 — and the one flag in this word that is NOT mandated zero in a query. In mDNS TC
means the known-answer list continues in a further message 400-500 ms behind this one, so it is
a thing the sender decides rather than a thing the format fixes.

nodes.purpose: RFC 6762 §7.2: more known answers follow in another message.

nodes.about: A bit holds nought or one.
RFC 6762 §18.6: Recursion Desired MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.
RFC 6762 §18.7: Recursion Available MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.
RFC 6762 §18.8: Zero MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.
RFC 6762 §18.9: Authentic Data MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.
RFC 6762 §18.10: Checking Disabled MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

RFC 6762 §18.11: MUST be zero on transmission, and a message with a non-zero RCODE MUST be silently ignored — responders that do not understand a query say nothing rather than answering with an error.

about: RFC 1035 §4.1.1. How many questions follow — and the only thing that says so, because a question
carries no terminator and the section that follows it looks exactly like another one.
Counted from the list going out and used to end the run coming in, so the header and the body
cannot disagree: there is one fact here and each direction reads it from whichever side knows.

nodes.about: Zero. A query MAY carry answers — RFC 6762 §7.1 calls it known-answer suppression, and it is how a querier says what it already holds so responders stay quiet. Carrying them needs the same count-driven repetition QDCOUNT does, so this description does not.

Zero in every mDNS query but one: RFC 6762 §8.2 puts the proposed records of a probe in the Authority section, which is how simultaneous probes are tie-broken. Probing is a lifecycle, not a message format, so it is not here.
Zero. No additional records in a plain query.

about: RFC 1035 §4.1.2: a name, a type, and a class — written once per question the caller asks.
How many there are is on the wire in QDCOUNT and nowhere else: a question carries no terminator,
and the section after the last one begins with a name exactly as another question would.
RFC 1035 §4.1.2 QNAME. A run of labels and then the root.
Two nodes rather than one, because that is what the octets are: the labels repeat and the root
does not. Making the root the last item of the repetition would write one per label.
One per label, and the repetition ends at a label whose length is zero.
That terminator is not a sentinel beside the run the way DHCP's end option is — it is the SAME
field reading zero. Which is why the reading looks at the next octet before committing to another
label: a length of zero is the root, and a length of anything else is another label. Nothing is
consumed by looking, so the root is then read by the node that owns it.
A run inside a run — the labels of THIS question — so what it is written once per item of is not
a list the caller hands in beside the questions, but one taken off the question being written.

nodes.about: RFC 1035 §4.1.4: the top two bits are zero for a label, so a length runs 1..63. Sixty-three rather than 255, and the two spare bits are what compression uses.
RFC 1035 §2.3.4: a label is 1 to 63 octets.
The label itself, as many octets as the length said. Text rather than octets, because a label is text — RFC 6763 §4.1 puts a human-readable instance name in one.

nodes.label: octets of label, from the length

nodes.purpose: What is being asked, one record per question. A name is its labels — ["_http", "_tcp", "local"] — rather than a dotted string, because a label may contain a dot and RFC 6763 §4.1 says instance names do.

nodes.label: the labels of this question's name
nodes.about: Read of the question being written, which is what makes the inner run this question's own rather than one flat list of labels with a scheme for telling which name each belongs to.
RFC 1035 §3.1: the null label of the root, which is what ends every name.
RFC 1035 §4.1.2. PTR is 12, which is what a DNS-SD browse asks for (RFC 6763 §4.1).

nodes.label: what kind of record this question wants

about: RFC 1035 §4.1.2 gives a sixteen-bit class; RFC 6762 §5.4 takes the top bit of it.
So it is two fields, not one integer with a note. A description that read 0x8001 as a class would
have to say in prose that the top bit means something else, and nothing could check it.

nodes.about: RFC 6762 §5.4: set to ask for a UNICAST reply. Recommended on the first query after startup, when the multicast cache of every other host on the link is of no use to a machine that has just arrived.

nodes.label: does this question want a direct answer?

nodes.about: RFC 1035 §3.2.4: 1 is IN. mDNS uses no other, but the field is fifteen bits wide and says so.

about: The reading's fork, and it is a look-ahead rather than a count because a name carries no count.
One octet, unconsumed: zero is the root and anything else is the length of another label. The
root is then read by its own node from its own octet, exactly as CoAP's payload is read after
the marker that announced it — a place never has to know that something looked before choosing
it.

nodes.about: Read ahead of deciding, from a copy of the position. Nothing is consumed.

about: Unlike the fork at the end of a name, this one counts — because QDCOUNT is the only thing that
says where the questions stop, and what follows a question looks exactly like another question.
`ordinal` is which time round THIS repetition is on, not how many times the walk has gone round
something. A name goes round inside a question, and a single counter shared by the walk would be
advanced by the labels and read here as though it counted questions.

nodes.about: Where a reading may stop. The questions go round, and a loop that has run out looks exactly like one that was cut short unless something says which endings were legal.

edges.because: RFC 6762 §5.1: this is the query format, so QR=1 is the response — which this description does not cover, and refuses rather than reads as a query with strange answers in it.
RFC 6762 §18.3: a query whose OPCODE is not zero MUST be silently ignored.
A bit holds nought or one.
RFC 6762 §18.11: a non-zero RCODE means this is not a message to act on.
RFC 6762 §7.1 known-answer suppression is outside what this describes — for the same reason QDCOUNT is one — so a query carrying answers is refused rather than read with them dropped.
RFC 6762 §8.2's probe carries its proposed records in the Authority section; this describes an ordinary query rather than a probe.
Nothing additional in a plain query.

Zero is the root and belongs to the root's own node. Sixty-four and above has one of the two top bits set, which RFC 1035 §4.1.4 reserves: 0xC0 begins a compression pointer, and a name ending in one is not something this can write — going out, where a thing sits is only settled after every value is, so no value can be derived from an offset.
A name ends at the root, and the root is the label of length nothing.
A bit holds nought or one.
